answers.explanation: Smaller broadcast domains, readable addresses, and a router between groups to filter traffic.
It has its own network address, broadcast address, and hosts. Routers treat it like any other network.
Things others must find (servers, printers, routers) are static. Short-stay client devices use DHCP.
The address is always 32 bits. Whatever the network ID gains, the host ID loses.
Location: building, floor, or site.
Three 1s in the last octet: 224.
A /23 holds 510; a /22 holds 1,022.
Classful protocols like RIPv1 didn't send masks, so 192.168.1.0/26 looked just like 192.168.1.0/24.
2² − 2 = 2. Under modern rules, all 4 are usable.
All 24 host bits are 1.
Block size 16. 18 is in the block at 16.
Block size 16 in the 3rd octet: this block runs from 16.0 to 31.255.
The second subnet is 10.1.1.64/26, which ends at .127.
Largest first. Big blocks need big aligned boundaries; small blocks fill in after.
Two usable hosts: one for each router.
A /28 starts on a multiple of 16: 0, 16, 32, 48...
The /25 ends at .127, and 128 is a multiple of 64.
Location is one signal at most. Each request is checked on identity, device health, and policy.
Policies tied to /25s, /28s, and /30s break or widen when a subnet is resized, which is why ZTA prefers identity-based policy.
/26 holds 62, too few; /25 holds 126.
